questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a court said about paying debts in paper
questions.learningObjective: Identify the holding of the 1870 decision on legal tender notes.
questions.stem: Reading the table on court rulings over paper money, which statement best describes the 1870 decision on legal tender?

options.text: The court held that paper notes issued by the federal government could lawfully pay any debt.
The court ruled that only debts owed to the government could be settled with paper notes.
options.misconception: Believes the ruling limited legal tender to public debts

options.text: The court struck down the paper money law because states could not regulate currency.
options.misconception: Thinks the case was about state control of money

options.text: The court postponed any ruling until the wartime inflation had already ended.
options.misconception: Assumes the court avoided deciding out of caution

questions.explanation: The 1870 decision upheld the wartime law, treating federal notes as lawful money for debts, public and private. Limiting it to public debts misreads the very holding it announced.
questions.hint: Focus on what the statute claimed and what the court affirmed.

questions.learningObjective: Explain what redemption power the 1870 ruling left in Congress's hands.

options.text: Congress could require any private bank to redeem its notes in silver on demand from the public.
options.misconception: Confuses Congress's preserved power with a rule about private banks

options.text: Congress could redeem the paper notes in lawful money, meaning gold or silver, at any time.
The court itself could order the Treasury to buy gold reserves before each payment was made.
options.misconception: Believes the court took over the Treasury's buying role

options.text: Congress could forbid the courts from hearing suits brought over questions of money.
options.misconception: Imagines the ruling silenced later lawsuits

questions.explanation: The court treated the notes as lawful money while leaving Congress's power to redeem them in coin untouched. The right preserved was Congress's, and it concerned redemption rather than tender status.
questions.hint: Focus on what the ruling said about coin, not about status.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The condition Congress put on issuing a note
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the redemption condition strengthened the standing of a federal note.
questions.stem: A note beneath the interest-rate table reads: notes shall be redeemable in lawful money at the office of the bank. Explain why that condition mattered.

answer.exemplar: Because every holder could take a note to the issuing bank and receive coin for it on demand, holders had a guarantee that the note was not merely a promise to pay someday. That convertibility at par is what gave national notes their acceptability in trade, and it is why merchants who insisted on metal were willing to take them.

questions.explanation: Redemption on demand in lawful money gave holders a guaranteed path to coin, so the notes were acceptable to those who insisted on metal. A promise to pay later, without that right, lacked the assurance.
questions.hint: Think about what the holder could actually do with the note.

options.misconception: Believes conversion wiped out all note taxes

options.text: It fixed the price of silver permanently by law for every year that followed.
options.misconception: Takes the promise for a lasting statutory price

options.text: It let lawmakers promise a future change in money without settling the silver question at once.

questions.learningObjective: Explain what the conditional silver clause accomplished for the coinage question.
questions.stem: The caption under the 1873 comparison table reads: silver dollars may be coined again if the metal reaches its old value. Explain what that clause accomplished.

answer.exemplar: The clause deferred the silver dispute by tying any change to a future market condition, so lawmakers could claim a safeguard for the coinage system while declining to commit to a new ratio or to new purchases. questions.explanation: Making any change conditional on the market avoided an immediate fight over the ratio or purchases. It bought time and political comfort without resolving what silver advocates had pressed since the early 1870s.
questions.hint: Ask what the condition postponed, not what it created.

questions.topic: The bond that stood behind a national bank note
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the deposit scheme preserved rather than replaced the gold standard.
questions.stem: Because the table notes what the statute did not do, why did the bond deposit scheme leave the gold standard intact rather than replacing it?

options.text: Because the deposit scheme made the notes themselves the reserve backing the gold that banks held.
options.misconception: Makes paper the reserve backing gold

options.text: Because the statute intended gold to be abandoned as soon as the first notes were issued.
options.misconception: Reads the scheme as an intended move off gold

options.text: Because the notes were redeemable in coin, so the pledge supported a convertibility promise instead of displacing the metal.
Because the statute said nothing about notes, and the deposit requirement came from a later law.
options.misconception: Claims the scheme postdates the statute it belongs to

questions.explanation: Making notes redeemable in coin meant paper rested on metal rather than replacing it, and the deposit guaranteed the government could meet redemptions. Aimed abandonment and paper as gold's reserve both fail.
questions.hint: Ask whether the notes displaced metal or rested on it.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The rate a law fixed for buying silver
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a change between two consecutive purchase figures.
questions.stem: Row six of the silver-purchase table shows two consecutive monthly figures. What does the change between them tell you?

options.text: The obligation was cut, because the later figure is stated in a different unit.
options.misconception: Confuses a change of unit with a change of size

options.text: The obligation had been repealed, because the later figure is the only one ever paid.
options.misconception: Reads one recorded payment as repeal

options.text: The obligation was unchanged, because both figures equal the same amount of silver.
options.misconception: Assumes the two figures are equal in metal

options.text: The obligation had been raised, because the later figure purchases more metal at any market price.

questions.explanation: A larger later figure means a bigger commitment, and more metal bought at any price marks that plainly. One payment does not repeal a duty, and a new unit changes the size only when the number rises.
questions.hint: Hold the market price constant and compare the numbers.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The condition Congress put on issuing a note
questions.learningObjective: Explain why redemption at par mattered to a note holder.
questions.stem: The caption beneath the interest comparison reads: the Treasurer shall redeem notes in lawful money at par. Explain why the words at par mattered.

answer.exemplar: Redeemable at par meant the holder received the full face value in coin, not a smaller sum that would reflect a market judgment about the bank or the government's credit. The phrase therefore made the redemption promise a promise about amount as well as about willingness, and it removed the discount that would otherwise have made redemption a poor substitute for simply holding the note.

questions.explanation: At par fixed the amount paid as the full face value, so redemption was a real alternative to holding the note. Without that word a holder could be offered less, and the promise would be worth much less.
questions.hint: Compare redemption at par with redemption below par.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The rate a law fixed for buying silver
questions.learningObjective: Apply the table's account of the notes issued for purchased silver.
questions.stem: Table six gathers the paper-money claims of the silver laws. Which statement about the notes issued for purchased silver is supported?

options.text: They were redeemable in the metal, and that feature was the reason silver advocates pressed for purchase.
They were the same paper money the 1862 act made lawful tender for all debts.
options.misconception: Merges the silver notes with the legal tender notes

options.text: They were redeemable only in silver and were forbidden from being paid in gold at all.
options.misconception: Invents a bar on gold redemption

options.text: They were issued to private refiners rather than to the public at large.
options.misconception: Redirects the notes to private buyers

questions.explanation: The table ties the silver notes to their metal and to the pressure behind purchases, without making them the general legal tender of 1862. Merging them with legal tender or barring gold misreads the column.
questions.hint: Check whether these notes were the general legal tender.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: A coinage promise that hid the price
questions.learningObjective: Sequence the stages of the country's silver legislation.
questions.stem: Order the table's four stages by date: the founding coinage act, the act that stopped silver coinage, the first purchase law, and the law that issued notes against silver.

options.text: The 1873 act, the founding act, the 1890 law, then the 1878 purchase law.
options.misconception: Moves the 1873 act ahead of the founding act

options.text: The founding act, the 1873 act, the 1878 purchase law, then the 1890 law that issued notes against silver.
The founding act, the 1878 purchase law, the 1873 act, then the 1890 law.
options.misconception: Swaps the 1873 and 1878 stages

options.text: The 1878 purchase law, the founding act, the 1873 act, then the 1890 law.
options.misconception: Starts the sequence with the 1878 law

questions.explanation: The founding act of 1792 came first, then the 1873 act stopped silver coinage, then the 1878 law began purchases, and the 1890 law issued notes against more metal. Every other order breaks that chronology.
questions.hint: Check the earliest date in the table before ordering.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a court said about paying debts in paper
questions.learningObjective: Infer the reasoning behind the legal tender holding from a quoted line.

stimulus.body: The notes were, in the judgment of the court, the proper paper money of the country, and the law which made them so was a legitimate exercise of the power of Congress.

questions.stem: A quoted line from the table's source book describes the notes as the country's proper paper money. What does the line imply about the ruling's reasoning?

options.text: The court treated the notes as a private convenience that Congress had no business creating.
options.misconception: Reads the ruling as a denial of congressional power

options.text: The court treated the notes as a temporary expedient that would be withdrawn once the war had ended.
options.misconception: Turns a legitimacy holding into a temporary measure

options.text: The court treated the notes as a legitimate national currency, so the dispute was about authority rather than value.
The court treated the notes as sound only if the government pledged all of its gold reserves.
options.misconception: Adds a gold pledge condition the opinion did not impose

questions.explanation: Calling the notes proper national paper money treats them as legitimate currency, locating the dispute in governmental authority rather than in the worth of paper. A temporary expedient misreads that.
questions.hint: Ask whether the court doubted the notes' legitimacy.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The concession a court made about payments in metal
questions.learningObjective: Weigh a reader's objection against the table's quoted holding.

stimulus.body: Petitioners argue that creditors must be restored the right to demand gold, and that paper promises should never discharge a debt.

questions.stem: A petition quoted above the table asks the court to protect creditors' right to demand gold. Which response does the table's own text support?

options.text: The court left the law exactly as it was, without ever ruling on the notes' status.
options.misconception: Denies that the court ruled on the notes' status

options.text: The court removed the redemption power entirely so that creditors could not obtain coin at all.
options.misconception: Overreads the preservation of redemption as its abolition

options.text: The court allowed creditors to demand gold in every case without any limit or exception.
options.misconception: Makes gold redemption a creditor's absolute right

options.text: The court left the government's power to redeem the notes in coin while still calling them lawful tender for debts.

questions.explanation: The quoted text calls the notes lawful tender while leaving redemption in coin to Congress. Abolishing redemption, granting creditors an unlimited right, and denying any opinion contradict it.
questions.hint: Note the two things the table's text does at once.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The bond that stood behind a national bank note
questions.learningObjective: Synthesize the two columns into the structural link they reveal.
questions.stem: The table splits the note issue into two columns. What overall pattern does the pairing support about how national money was created?

options.text: Notes were created by banks acting on their own credit alone, with the bond column merely decorative.
options.misconception: Treats the bond column as an afterthought

options.text: Notes were created only as claims on pledged government bonds, so public credit and private currency were tied together.
Notes were created by the Treasury directly, so the bond column reflects a later accounting entry.
options.misconception: Makes the Treasury the sole issuer

options.text: Notes were created by state legislatures, so the bond column tracks state rather than federal pledges.
options.misconception: Reassigns the pledges to the states

questions.explanation: The pairing shows private banks creating money only against public securities, the link the table records. Bank credit alone, direct Treasury issue, and state pledges each break that connection.
questions.hint: Ask which side of the pair created the money.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The condition Congress put on issuing a note
questions.learningObjective: Judge which requirement a bank faced as a binding cost.
questions.stem: Read the interest rate before the reserve rule, then identify which of the two the bank faced as a cost of doing business.

options.text: Neither mattered, since national banks could hold their reserves in anything convenient to them.
options.misconception: Claims the reserve rule left reserves unconstrained

options.text: The rate was the binding cost, and the reserve rule merely told banks what to do with any surplus.
options.misconception: Turns a binding requirement into an optional instruction

options.text: The reserve rule made holding lawful money a binding requirement, whatever the rate on the reserve paper earned.
The reserve rule was a tax, so the rate played no part in the bank's costs at all.
options.misconception: Recasts a reserve requirement as a levy

questions.explanation: A reserve requirement binds regardless of what the reserve paper earns, so it is a bank's standing cost. Calling the rate the binding cost, freeing reserves, or treating the rule as a tax misstates it.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two could a bank refuse?
